title: Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023, Datasets and Benchmarks Track)
problem_statement: Investigates how disparities in the treatment of different languages arise at the subword tokenization stage before a language model is even invoked, leading to severe inflation in sequence lengths across languages.
domain: Natural Language Processing, Subword Tokenization, Multilingual NLP Fairness
theoretical_framework: Information-theoretic tokenization efficiency and multilingual tokenization parity; analysis of Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and WordPiece fertility disparities across Latin and non-Latin scripts.
methodology: Evaluates tokenization lengths, fertility metrics, and character-to-token ratios across multiple commercial and open-source tokenizers (including GPT-2, GPT-4, LLaMA, XLM-R, and mT5) on parallel multilingual corpora spanning typologically diverse languages.
evaluation: Sequence tokenization length ratio relative to English
API pricing cost multiplier across languages
Context window saturation rate and generation latency
key_findings: The same text translated into different languages produces drastically different tokenization lengths, exceeding 2x to 7x inflation for low-resource languages and up to 15x in extreme cases.
Subword tokenizers disproportionately segment non-English and low-resource words into character-level fragments, creating a tokenization parity premium.
Over-fragmentation directly inflates downstream inference latency, increases per-query API costs, and prematurely exhausts model context windows for non-English speakers.
Multilingual tokenizers trained without explicit language-balancing constraints still exhibit substantial tokenization length disparities across language families.
scope_and_delimitations: Examines subword and byte-level tokenization algorithms across commercial LLM APIs and pre-trained open multilingual encoders on parallel translated benchmarks.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: While we propose vocabulary balancing, our experiments do not evaluate whether increasing vocabulary allocation for under-represented languages negatively impacts the representation capacity of the core pre-training language.
limitations.summary: The study evaluates tokenization length and pricing fairness across languages but does not train end-to-end downstream models to measure the exact downstream task accuracy trade-offs of vocabulary re-allocation.

generalizability_gap: Evaluates parallel sentence translations across standard national languages; untested on informal intra-sentential code-switched microblogs or regional agglutinative dialects such as Taglish.
methodological_gap: Focuses primarily on fertility ratios and cost metrics rather than directly measuring gradient variance or representation dilution in multi-task loss landscapes.
future_work: Developing multilingually fair subword tokenizers with equitable fertility across language families.
Investigating downstream task performance under balanced multilingual tokenization budgets.
